title: Tanwīn — the three nunation marks
objectives: Student can name and point to the three tanwīn marks — ـٌ ـً ـٍ — and say the sound each one adds: -un, -an, -in.
Student can read a fully-vowelled noun carrying any of the three, producing the n sound without hunting the page for a written ن.
Student can explain that the alif written under a fatḥatān (كِتَابًا) is a carrier and is NOT lengthened when reading on.
Student can read a shuffled column of 20 nouns marked with all three tanwīns at roughly one word per two seconds, with no warm-up cue.

slides.heading: Lesson 2.1 — Tanwīn: the three nunation marks
Read this
body: كِتَابًا. Read it out loud before anything is explained.
Most students who have finished an alphabet course do one of two things here. Either they hunt the page for a ن that is not there and stall, or they see the alif and stretch it: ‘ki-taa-baa’.
Both come from the same wrong assumption: that Arabic writes every sound as a letter. It does not.
The right reading is kitāban — ‘a book’. There is an n in it, and no ن on the page.

audio.cue: كِتَابًا: kitāban, ‘a book’. Two fatḥas on the ب add the n. The alif after it is silent — do not stretch it.

slides.heading: Doubling the mark adds an n
body: Tanwīn (nunation — ‘adding a nūn’) is the third thing a final vowel can do. It is the same three harakāt (short-vowel marks) you already know, drawn twice.
One ḍamma is ‘bu’. Two ḍammas is ‘bun’.
One kasra is ‘bi’. Two kasras is ‘bin’.
One fatḥa is ‘ba’. Two fatḥas is ‘ban’.
Doubling the mark adds an n. That is the entire rule.

audio.cue: بُ: one ḍamma — bu.
بٌ: two ḍammas — bun. Doubling the mark added the n.
بِ: one kasra — bi.
بٍ: two kasras — bin.
بَ: one fatḥa — ba.
بً: two fatḥas — ban.

slides.heading: The three names, said once
body: ـٌ is ḍammatān — ‘two ḍammas’. It reads -un.
ـٍ is kasratān — ‘two kasras’. It reads -in.
ـً is fatḥatān — ‘two fatḥas’. It reads -an.
Learn the names so you recognise them from a teacher or a book, then use plain English for the rest of the lesson. The names are not the skill; the reading is.

slides.heading: The n you can see, and the n you cannot
body: You have read مِنْ (min — ‘from’) since Unit 1.4. Its n is a written letter.
بَابٍ (bābin — ‘a door’) ends in exactly the same sound. Its n is a mark.
Say the pair aloud several times: min … bābin … min … bābin.
No new sound has been introduced today — only a new way of writing a sound you can already make. Stop looking for the ن.

audio.cue: مِنْ: min, ‘from’. The n here is a written letter, closed by a sukūn.
بَابٍ: bābin, ‘a door’. The n here is the second kasra. Same sound, no letter.

slides.heading: The carrying alif is a chair, not a sound
body: Fatḥatān almost always needs something to sit on, so an alif is written after the last letter purely to hold it.
That alif is silent when you carry on reading. بَابًا read into the next word is bāban, not bābā.
Two spellings take no extra alif at all: a word ending in tāʾ marbūṭah (the tied ة) — سَاعَةً, sāʿatan — and a word already ending in a hamza on the line after an alif — مَاءً, māʾan.
You do not need to predict which is which. Recognition only: if you see ـًا, do not lengthen it.

audio.cue: بَابًا: bāban. Cover the alif with a fingertip — it is a chair for the mark, not a sound.
سَاعَةً: sāʿatan, ‘an hour’. Fatḥatān on a tāʾ marbūṭah — no carrying alif needed.
مَاءً: māʾan, ‘water’. The word already ends in a hamza after an alif, so no extra alif is written.

slides.heading: Where tanwīn is allowed — and where today stops
body: Only on nouns and adjectives, and only on the last letter of the word. A verb never takes it.
Nothing follows a tanwīn inside a word. If you think you have found one in the middle of a word, you have misread a shadda or a plain fatḥa — and both of those are lessons ahead of this one.
What that unwritten n does to the letter that follows it — sometimes hidden, sometimes hummed, sometimes swapped for an m — is the largest single topic in Unit 3.
Today the n is a clean, plain n every time. Do not go looking further.

slides.instructions: Read each pair, left then right, six times. Both halves end in the same sound. If the second half sounds shorter or weaker than the first, you are under-saying the tanwīn.

audio.cue: مِنْ … بَابٍ: min … bābin. Written n, then unwritten n. Identical sound.

كُنْ … وَلَدًا: kun … waladan. Written n, then unwritten n on a fatḥatān.
إِنْ … دَرْسٌ: in … darsun. Written n, then unwritten n on a ḍammatān.

slides.heading: Five real anchors — read them, do not analyse them
body: Everything else in this lesson is ordinary Arabic vocabulary, deliberately: you need volume and shuffling today more than you need reverence.
These five are from the Qurʾān, one for each mark. Read them straight through.

audio.cue: أَحَدٌ (112:1): ḍammatān — aḥadun. Two ḍammas, one unwritten n.
لَهَبٍ (111:1): kasratān — lahabin.
سِجِّيلٍ (105:4): kasratān — sijjīlin.
يُسْرًا (94:5): fatḥatān on a carrying alif — yusran. The alif is silent when you continue.
ثَجَّاجًا (78:14): fatḥatān, same carrying alif — thajjājan.
بٌ: two ḍammas — bun.
بً: two fatḥas — ban.
بٍ: two kasras — bin.
بَابٌ: bābun.
بَابًا: bāban — the alif is silent.
بَابٍ: bābin.
مِنْ: min. The written n, for comparison — it sounds no different.

slides.heading: Homework — 15–20 min/day, five days
tasks: Three minutes — the marks alone. Write ـٌ ـً ـٍ on a scrap of paper and say the sound of each, in a shuffled order, until you never hesitate.
Five minutes — Drill 1 aloud, all six rows read across. Record thirty seconds of it on your phone, play it back, and check every word ends in an audible n.
Five minutes — Drill 5 cold read. Time yourself on the second run only; do not chase the clock before day three.
Three minutes — Drill 3, the silent alif. Put a fingertip over each carrying alif as you read.
Write four words. Copy any four words from Drill 5 by hand and put a different tanwīn on each one — writing the mark is what stops you confusing ـً with a plain fatḥa.
Bring to the next session: the one word from Drill 5 you got wrong most often, and whether the error was the n or the alif.

dailyChecklist: Three minutes on the marks alone — ـٌ ـً ـٍ shuffled, until there is no hesitation
Drill 1 aloud, all six rows across; record thirty seconds and check every word ends in an audible n
Drill 5 cold read, timed on the second run only
Drill 3 with a fingertip over each carrying alif
Copy four words from Drill 5 by hand, putting a different tanwīn on each

script: Lead with the error, out loud, before you define anything. Ask her to read كِتَابًا. Say the wrong version deliberately — ki-taa-baa — then the right one — kitāban — and ask which one has an n in it. Only then show the mark.

Anchor on the shape, not the name. Write بُ, then بٌ, and ask what changed. She will say ‘there are two now’. Confirm it, supply the sound, and repeat for kasra and fatḥa. Doubling the mark adds an n; that is the entire rule and it takes ninety seconds.
Give the names — ḍammatān, fatḥatān, kasratān — once, so she recognises them from a teacher or a book, then drop them and use plain English for the rest of the lesson.
Kill the missing-nūn hunt immediately. Write مِنْ and بَابٍ side by side and say the pair aloud several times: min … bābin … min … bābin. She must hear that no new sound has been introduced today.

Give the carrying alif a whole step of its own. Write بَابًا, cover the alif with a fingertip, and have her read it again. Mention the two no-alif spellings — سَاعَةً and مَاءً — as recognition only; she does not need to predict which is which.
State where tanwīn is allowed: nouns and adjectives, last letter only, never a verb, nothing after it inside a word.

Flag forward, then close the door. What the unwritten n does to the following letter is the largest topic in Unit 3. Say the sentence, do not demonstrate it, and do not answer the follow-up beyond ‘Unit 3’.
Gate for the teacher: do not start lesson 2-02 in the same session if the carrying alif is still being lengthened. Drill 3 is the pass condition — six clean -an endings in a row, twice.

listenFor.item: The n of any tanwīn, produced without a written ن on the page
listenFor.commonMistake: Hunting for a nūn — a half-second stall at the end of the word, eyes moving back over the last letter, then the word restarted.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Every previous lesson taught one sound per letter. Tanwīn is the first sound in the course with no letter of its own, so she is doing exactly what she was trained to do.
listenFor.correctionCue: ‘The n is in the mark, not in a letter. Two of anything means n.’

listenFor.item: The carrying alif under a fatḥatān, silent when reading on — kitāban, not kitābā
listenFor.commonMistake: An open ā at the end of the word with no consonant closing it.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Alif has meant ‘long a’ in every word she has read so far. This is the first time it means nothing.
listenFor.correctionCue: ‘That alif is a chair for the mark to sit on. Close the word with an n.’ Cover the alif with a fingertip and have her read the word again.

listenFor.item: The n held to full strength through a long column
listenFor.commonMistake: Under-saying the n until it disappears — bābu instead of bābun, especially by the third or fourth word of a column.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Nothing on the page enforces it, so it is the first thing to be dropped once concentration slips.
listenFor.correctionCue: ‘I heard bābu. Where did the n go?’ Then re-run the مِنْ / بَابٍ pair from Drill 2 — hearing the written n next to the unwritten one restores it faster than any explanation.

listenFor.item: The word stopping dead on the n, with no vowel after it
listenFor.commonMistake: Adding a vowel after the n — bābuna. An extra beat at the end of the word; a two-syllable ending where there should be one.
listenFor.whyItHappens: The same reflex that puts a helper vowel after a sukūn, diagnosed in lesson 1-13. It is one habit, not two.
listenFor.correctionCue: ‘Stop the sound dead on the n.’ Clap on the stop and have her land on your clap — the same diagnostic she already knows from sukūn.

listenFor.item: Fatḥatān read as -an, not -am and not a bare -a
listenFor.commonMistake: A lip closure at the end of the word, or no consonant at all.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Fatḥatān is the least visually distinct of the three, and it is the only one with an extra letter next to it — so it gets guessed at.
listenFor.correctionCue: ‘All three tanwīns end in the same letter sound. Only the vowel before it changes.’

teacherNotes.homework: 15–20 min/day, five days. Three minutes on the marks alone (ـٌ ـً ـٍ shuffled until there is no hesitation). Five minutes on Drill 1 read across, with thirty seconds recorded and played back to check every word ends in an audible n. Five minutes on the Drill 5 cold read, timed on the second run only and not chasing the clock before day three. Three minutes on Drill 3 with a fingertip over each carrying alif. Then copy four words from Drill 5 by hand, putting a different tanwīn on each — writing the mark is what stops her confusing ـً with a plain fatḥa. She brings back the word she got wrong most often and whether the error was the n or the alif.
